# GitHub PR Review Analysis

Use this skill to turn noisy GitHub PR review feedback into a clear action plan.

> **Core insight:** GitHub review queues contain a mix of real blockers, stale noise, personal preference, and already-resolved discussion. The job is not to summarize everything. The job is to surface the comments that still deserve action.

## Goal

Fetch all relevant review feedback from a PR, filter out resolved or stale noise, and categorize the remaining comments into:

- Must Do
- Consider
- Safely Ignore

The value of this skill is judgment, not just retrieval. The user should come away knowing what is actually blocking, what is worth considering, and what can be skipped.

## When to use this skill

Use this skill when the user wants to:

- triage GitHub PR review comments
- decide which comments are actually blocking
- understand whether review feedback is stale, resolved, or still relevant
- convert review noise into a prioritized fix list
- draft short, respectful replies to review threads

Do not use this skill for general code review of a branch with no PR review feedback yet. This skill is specifically for analyzing existing GitHub review comments and threads.

## Inputs to support

Accept PR references in any of these forms:

- `owner/repo#123`
- `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123`
- `#123` when already inside the repo

If the reference is ambiguous, resolve it before continuing.

If the user does not provide a PR reference but the current repo context strongly suggests one, ask one short clarifying question instead of guessing.

## Preflight

Before doing any analysis:

1. Confirm you can identify `owner`, `repo`, and PR `number`.
2. Confirm `gh` access works.
3. Stay read-only throughout.

Use `gh` for GitHub access. If authentication or repo access fails, stop and report the problem clearly.

## Tooling guidance

- Use `gh` via the shell for GitHub data retrieval.
- Stay read-only.
- When inspecting local code, prefer dedicated file tools for reading and searching rather than shell text-processing commands.
- Read the narrowest relevant diff or file context before judging a comment.

## Core workflow

1. Parse the PR reference.
2. Fetch PR metadata for title, status, author, base branch, and head branch.
3. Fetch review threads and top-level reviews with `gh` so you can reliably inspect:
   - `isResolved`
   - `isOutdated`
   - review `state`
4. Filter out noise:
   - resolved threads
   - outdated threads
   - CI/tooling bot comments (but keep AI reviewer bot comments — see filtering rules)
   - pure praise with no action requested
5. Read the full surviving thread context before judging any comment.
6. Inspect the relevant code or diff when a comment references a file or line.
7. Judge whether the concern still applies to the current PR state.
8. Categorize each remaining comment into exactly one tier.
9. Produce the final report in the required format.

## Retrieval workflow

Prefer GraphQL for thread-aware review analysis because thread resolution and outdated state are necessary for correct triage.

### 1. Confirm access

```bash
gh auth status
```

### 2. Fetch PR metadata

```bash
gh pr view <number> --repo <owner/repo> --json title,body,state,baseRefName,headRefName,author,mergeable
```

### 3. Fetch reviews and review threads

Use GraphQL, not the REST API, because thread resolution and outdated state are critical to correct triage.

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner: String!, $repo: String!, $number: Int!) {
  repository(owner: $owner, name: $repo) {
    pullRequest(number: $number) {
      title
      state
      reviews(first: 100) {
        nodes {
          author { login }
          state
          body
          createdAt
          url
        }
      }
      reviewThreads(first: 100) {
        nodes {
          isResolved
          isOutdated
          comments(first: 50) {
            nodes {
              author { login }
              body
              path
              line
              createdAt
              url
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -f owner="<owner>" -f repo="<repo>" -F number=<number>
```

If there are more than 100 reviews or threads, paginate with `endCursor` and `hasNextPage` until all data is collected.

If you need changed-file context, fetch file metadata too:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --repo <owner/repo> --json files
```

Do not stop at top-level review summaries. A correct analysis requires thread-level context.

## Filtering rules

Exclude comments or threads that should not be actioned:

- Threads with `isResolved: true`
- Threads with `isOutdated: true`
- CI/tooling bot authors (filter these out entirely):
  - `github-actions[bot]`
  - `codecov[bot]`
  - `dependabot[bot]`
  - `sonarcloud[bot]`
  - `renovate[bot]`
  - any `[bot]` login that only posts CI status, coverage, or dependency updates
- Comments that are only praise or acknowledgment, such as:
  - `LGTM`
  - `Looks good!`
  - `Nice work`

**Do not filter out AI reviewer bots.** The following are AI-powered code reviewers whose comments should be analyzed by technical merit like any other reviewer:

- `copilot-pull-request-reviewer[bot]` (GitHub Copilot)
- `coderabbitai[bot]` (CodeRabbit)
- `sourcery-ai[bot]` (Sourcery)
- `ellipsis-dev[bot]` (Ellipsis)
- Any `[bot]` login that posts line-level code review comments with technical substance

When you encounter an unfamiliar `[bot]` author, inspect the comment content before deciding:

- If the comment is a CI status check, coverage report, or dependency alert → filter it out.
- If the comment is a line-level code review with technical feedback (bug, suggestion, question) → keep it and analyze it normally.

When in doubt about a bot author, keep the comment and analyze it. It is better to include a low-value AI comment in `Safely Ignore` with an explanation than to silently discard a valid finding.

Also treat a thread as effectively resolved if the back-and-forth clearly shows the concern was addressed, even if GitHub still shows it as unresolved.

Be conservative with this rule. Only mark an unresolved thread as effectively resolved when the thread itself contains strong evidence that the concern was handled.

## How to analyze surviving comments

For each remaining item, evaluate:

- Who left it
- Whether it came from a `CHANGES_REQUESTED`, `COMMENTED`, or `APPROVED` review
- Whether it is a bug, concern, question, suggestion, nit, or preference
- Whether the comment is technically valid
- Whether there is a concrete action the PR author can take
- Whether the impact is correctness, security, performance, maintainability, readability, or style only

Also evaluate:

- Whether the reviewer is reacting to old code that has already changed
- Whether the suggestion conflicts with visible project conventions
- Whether the thread contains clarification that narrows or softens the original ask
- Whether the user asked for triage only, or also wants suggested reply language

### Severity guidance

- Comments inside a `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review deserve more weight because the reviewer explicitly signaled blocking intent.
- Comments inside an `APPROVED` review are often non-blocking unless they identify a real correctness or safety issue.
- If a suggestion is weak, subjective, or based on a misunderstanding, do not inflate it.
- A technically valid comment can still belong in `Consider` if the impact is low.
- A reviewer's blocking intent matters, but technical merit matters more.

## Code inspection guidance

When a comment references a file or line, inspect the current diff or local code before judging it.

Prefer the narrowest useful context:

```bash
gh pr diff <number> --repo <owner/repo>
```

Then inspect the referenced file or surrounding code in the local repo when available.

Only use broader PR context when the comment depends on cross-file behavior.

Use local file reads or search when helpful, but remember the PR diff is often the most reliable source for what the reviewer actually commented on.

If you cannot inspect the relevant code, say so and lower confidence rather than pretending certainty.

## Categorization rules

Place every analyzed comment into exactly one category.

### Must Do

Use only for genuinely blocking issues, such as:

- bugs
- correctness problems
- security vulnerabilities
- data loss risks
- explicit request-changes items with strong technical basis

Keep this category strict. If ignoring the comment would not cause real harm, it probably does not belong here.

Use `Must Do` only when you can explain the concrete downside of not fixing it.

### Consider

Use for non-blocking but worthwhile feedback, such as:

- valid improvement ideas
- low-impact bugs
- readability improvements
- convention-backed consistency fixes
- reasonable questions that need answers

When unsure, prefer `Consider` over `Safely Ignore`.

### Safely Ignore

Use for comments that are not worth actioning, such as:

- pure nitpicks without substance
- subjective preferences with no project convention behind them
- incorrect suggestions
- comments based on misunderstanding
- redundant feedback already covered elsewhere

If multiple comments raise the same issue, keep the strongest representative item and note duplicates briefly instead of repeating the same concern many times.

## Confidence and disagreement handling

When the evidence is mixed:

- Say what is clear
- Say what is uncertain
- Prefer `Consider` over `Must Do`
- Explain the missing evidence that would change the call

If reviewer intent and technical merit diverge, optimize for technical merit while acknowledging reviewer intent.

Examples:

- `CHANGES_REQUESTED` + weak stylistic preference -> usually `Consider` or `Safely Ignore`
- `APPROVED` + real correctness issue -> can still be `Must Do`

## Optional reply help

If the user wants help replying to review comments, add a short follow-up section after the triage report:

```markdown
## Suggested Replies

- **@reviewer**: <brief respectful reply>
```

Keep replies factual, calm, and specific. Do not be defensive.

## Report format

Use this exact structure:

```markdown
# PR Review Analysis: <PR title> (#<number>)

**PR:** <owner/repo>#<number>
**Status:** <open/merged/closed>
**Author:** @<author>
**Base:** <base> <- <head>

**Filtered out:** X resolved threads · Y outdated threads · Z CI/tooling bot comments
**AI reviewers included:** <list logins, or "none">
**Analyzed:** N comments across M threads
**Confidence:** <high/medium/low>

---

## Must Do (N)

> Blocking issues that should be addressed before merge

### 1. [<file>:<line>] <Brief summary>

**Reviewer:** @<login>
**Type:** <bug/security/correctness/data-loss>

> <Original comment text, quoted>

**Why this matters:** <1-2 sentence explanation of the real impact>
**Suggested action:** <What specifically to do>

---

## Consider (N)

> Non-blocking but worth reviewing — good suggestions that improve quality

### 1. [<file>:<line>] <Brief summary>

**Reviewer:** @<login>
**Type:** <improvement/style/readability/question>

> <Original comment text, quoted>

**Why:** <Brief rationale for why it's worth considering>

---

## Safely Ignore (N)

> Nitpicks, incorrect suggestions, or subjective preferences

### 1. [<file>:<line>] <Brief summary>

**Reviewer:** @<login>

> <Original comment text, quoted>

**Why safe to skip:** <Brief reason>

---

_Analysis complete. Comments are categorized by impact — verify "Must Do" items first._
```

If a tier has no items, still include the header and write:

```markdown
No items in this category.
```

If no comments survive filtering, use:

```markdown
# PR Review Analysis: <PR title> (#<number>)

**PR:** <owner/repo>#<number>
**Status:** <open/merged/closed>

**Filtered out:** X resolved · Y outdated · Z CI/tooling bot comments

## All Clear

No actionable unresolved comments remain on this PR. All review threads are either resolved, outdated, or addressed in conversation.
```

## Error handling

- If `gh` is not authenticated, report: `Error: gh CLI is not authenticated. Run gh auth login to authenticate.`
- If the PR cannot be accessed, report: `Error: Could not access PR <reference>. Verify the PR exists and you have access.`
- If the PR has no review comments at all, report: `This PR has no review comments.`
- If the PR reference is ambiguous, ask one concise clarifying question before doing more work.
- Handle GraphQL pagination silently and continue until all relevant data is gathered.

## Guardrails

- Stay read-only.
- Never push code.
- Never approve or dismiss reviews.
- Never resolve conversations.
- Never fabricate comments or thread state.
- Always quote the original comment text so the user can verify your judgment.
- Do not overuse `Must Do`.
- Do not confuse reviewer preference with project requirement unless you have evidence of a convention.
- Do not claim a comment is stale or resolved without evidence from thread state, thread content, or current code.

The user is relying on triage quality. Be skeptical of weak feedback, but cautious about missing real blockers.

description: Use when working with the internal shared GKE Kubernetes cluster, kubectl investigation, Argo CD GitOps delivery, Helm and Kustomize manifests, Gateway API HTTPRoutes, GKE external load balancer backends, IAP-secured services, Workload Identity, Secret Manager secret sync, resource tuning, or Kubernetes troubleshooting. Favor repo-managed declarative changes over live cluster mutation.
---

# Kubernetes Specialist

Senior Kubernetes engineer for the shared internal GKE platform. Treat the cluster as GitOps-managed infrastructure: inspect live state when needed, but make durable changes in the owning repository and let Argo CD reconcile them.

## Internal Platform Profile

- Shared GKE cluster for many teams and applications, with cluster and network primitives managed separately from application manifests.
- Argo CD owns deployment reconciliation. Application work should flow through Git, pull request review, and Argo CD sync status.
- Helm and Kustomize are both first-class. Prefer existing base/overlay/component patterns instead of inventing parallel structure.
- North-south traffic uses Gateway API on a GKE global external managed load balancer. Application exposure normally uses `HTTPRoute` plus GKE backend policies.
- IAP, health checks, timeouts, certificates, DNS, Workload Identity, Secret Manager sync, and shared network concerns may span Kubernetes and foundation infrastructure. Identify the owning layer before editing.

## Core Workflow

1. **Identify ownership** — Determine whether the change belongs in app GitOps manifests, shared platform services, or cluster/network infrastructure. Do not patch live resources as the primary fix.
2. **Read nearby examples first** — Match existing app layout, labels, namespace conventions, Argo CD waves, Kustomize patches, Helm chart usage, and Gateway API patterns.
3. **Inspect live state safely** — Use read-only `kubectl`, `argocd`, and `gcloud` commands to confirm the current context, resource status, events, routes, and backend health.
4. **Change declaratively** — Update base/overlay manifests, Helm values, Kustomize patches, or infrastructure code in the owning repo. Keep environment-specific values in overlays.
5. **Validate locally** — Render manifests before handoff: `kustomize build --enable-helm <overlay>` or the repo wrapper if present. Run schema/lint tools when configured.
6. **Verify reconciliation** — Check Argo CD sync/health and Kubernetes rollout status after merge/sync. Investigate drift rather than force-applying over it.

### Error Recovery

- **Argo CD OutOfSync:** Compare desired vs live resource, inspect diff, fix the owning manifest, then sync. Avoid `kubectl apply` bandaids.
- **Degraded app:** Check `Application` health, rollout status, pod events, logs, probes, SecretSync state, and backend health. Fix the smallest durable cause.
- **Gateway route failure:** Check `HTTPRoute` `Accepted` / `ResolvedRefs`, parent `Gateway` listener, hostname, backend `Service` port, `HealthCheckPolicy`, and `GCPBackendPolicy`.
- **IAP access issue:** Confirm backend policy enables IAP, identity access is granted in the owning infrastructure layer, and the request is using the expected host/backend.

## Reference Guide

Load detailed guidance based on context:

| Topic              | Reference                        | Load When                                                                     |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| GitOps workflow    | `references/gitops.md`           | Argo CD apps, sync drift, repo ownership, promotion                           |
| Helm + Kustomize   | `references/helm-kustomize.md`   | App structure, overlays, chart values, patches                                |
| Gateway API        | `references/gateway-api.md`      | HTTPRoute, Gateway listeners, load balancer, IAP, backend policies            |
| Secrets + identity | `references/secrets-identity.md` | Secret Manager sync, SecretProviderClass, Workload Identity, service accounts |
| Troubleshooting    | `references/troubleshooting.md`  | kubectl/argocd investigation and verification commands                        |

## Constraints

### MUST DO

- Confirm the current `kubectl` context before inspecting cluster state.
- Prefer read-only live commands unless the user explicitly asks for an emergency mutation.
- Make durable changes in GitOps or infrastructure code, not by hand-editing live resources.
- Use Kustomize overlays for environment-specific hostnames, routes, chart values, and generated config.
- Pin Helm chart versions and preserve existing `includeCRDs`, `skipTests`, and values-file conventions.
- Use Gateway API `HTTPRoute` resources for external HTTP(S) exposure.
- Add or update `GCPBackendPolicy` for backend timeouts and IAP behavior when the service requires it.
- Add or update `HealthCheckPolicy` when default load-balancer health checks do not match the app.
- Keep secrets out of Git; use Secret Manager sync patterns and runtime-populated Kubernetes Secrets.
- Use Workload Identity annotations and least-privilege service accounts when workloads access Google Cloud APIs.

### MUST NOT DO

- Do not commit kubeconfigs, credentials, rendered secret values, or plaintext `Secret` data.
- Do not introduce legacy `Ingress` for external app routes unless the existing app already requires it.
- Do not create one-off namespaces, Gateways, or load balancers when the shared platform primitive already exists.
- Do not use `kubectl apply`, `kubectl edit`, `kubectl patch`, or Argo CD force sync as a durable fix.
- Do not use `latest` image tags, unpinned chart versions, or broad RBAC.
- Do not change cluster/network foundation resources for an app-only issue without proving ownership.

## Output Expectations

When implementing Kubernetes changes, provide:

1. Files changed and why each layer owns the change.
2. Render/validation command output, or a clear reason it could not be run.
3. Argo CD and `kubectl` verification commands for the user to run after merge/sync.
4. Any cross-layer dependencies, such as DNS, IAP IAM, certificates, or infrastructure changes.

name: merge-pr
description: >-
  Merge GitHub pull requests safely using gh, always rebasing the source branch
  onto the destination branch first, then squash merging with a conventional
  commit title that ends in the PR number, a cleaned-up commit body, and no co-author trailers.
  Use whenever the user asks to merge a PR, land a pull request, squash a PR,
  clean up a merge commit message, or remove co-authored-by lines from a GitHub
  PR merge, even if they do not explicitly say "squash."
---

# Merge PR

## Overview

Use this skill to land GitHub PRs with consistent commit history: first rebase the source branch on the destination branch, then create one squash commit with a conventional commit title, the PR number suffix, a concise human-written body, and no `Co-authored-by:` trailers.

The default posture is cautious: inspect first, merge only after the PR is mergeable and the user has clearly asked to merge it.

## Required behavior

- Always use GitHub CLI (`gh`) for GitHub operations.
- Always rebase the PR source branch onto the destination branch immediately before squash merging.
- Reconcile rebase conflicts before merging. If the rebase rewrites the source branch, push it with `--force-with-lease`.
- Always squash merge. Never create a merge commit or rebase merge.
- Always use a conventional commit title ending with the PR number in parentheses: `<type>(<scope>): <summary> (#<PR>)` or `<type>: <summary> (#<PR>)`.
- Always clean the commit body before merging.
- Always remove `Co-authored-by:` trailers and any prose that describes co-authors.
- Do not push, force-push, close, edit, or merge anything other than the requested PR source branch.
- Never force-push the destination branch. Only use `git push --force-with-lease` for the PR source branch after a successful rebase.
- If the target PR is ambiguous, ask one short clarifying question.

## Inputs to support

Accept PR references in any of these forms:

- `owner/repo#123`
- `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123`
- `#123` when already inside the repository
- no argument, when the current branch has exactly one associated PR

If no PR is provided, resolve the PR for the current branch:

```bash
gh pr view --json number,url,headRefName,baseRefName,state,isDraft,mergeable,title,body,statusCheckRollup
```

If no PR exists or more than one PR is plausible, stop and ask which PR to merge.

## Preflight

Before merging:

1. Confirm `gh` is authenticated and can access the repo.
2. Fetch PR metadata.
3. Verify the PR is open and not a draft.
4. Verify it is mergeable or report the merge-blocking reason.
5. Inspect status checks and warn if required checks are failing or pending.
6. Confirm the source branch can be checked out locally and safely rebased.
7. Inspect the PR title/body and commits enough to draft a clean squash commit message.
8. Show the final title and body to the user before merging unless the user explicitly requested a fully automated merge.

Useful commands:

```bash
gh auth status
gh pr view <number> --repo <owner/repo> --json url,number,title,body,state,isDraft,mergeable,baseRefName,headRefName,author,commits,statusCheckRollup,reviewDecision
```

## Rebase the source branch first

Immediately before squash merging, rebase the PR source branch onto the latest destination branch. This keeps the destination branch history clean and ensures the final squash commit is based on current destination state.

Use a local checkout of the PR branch:

```bash
gh pr checkout <number> --repo <owner/repo>
git fetch origin <base-branch>
git rebase origin/<base-branch>
```

If the rebase succeeds and rewrote commits, update the PR source branch:

```bash
git push --force-with-lease origin HEAD:<head-branch>
```

Conflict handling:

- Stop and inspect each conflict. Resolve from first principles, preserving both the PR intent and destination branch changes.
- Run the relevant formatter/tests for files touched while resolving conflicts.
- Continue with `git rebase --continue` until the rebase completes.
- If the conflict cannot be resolved confidently, stop and explain the blocking files and choices.
- After a successful conflict resolution rebase, push with `--force-with-lease` to the PR source branch.

Safety rules:

- Never use plain `--force`; use `--force-with-lease` only.
- Never force-push `main`, `master`, or the destination branch.
- If the PR source branch is from a fork and cannot be pushed, report that the branch must be updated by the PR author before merging.
- After pushing the rebased source branch, refetch PR metadata and re-check mergeability/status checks before merging.

## Conventional commit title

Draft a title from the PR title, branch name, commit subjects, and changed-files context. Always append the PR number suffix: ` (#<PR>)`.

Allowed common types:

- `feat`: new user-facing capability
- `fix`: bug fix
- `docs`: documentation only
- `test`: tests only or test infrastructure
- `refactor`: behavior-preserving code restructuring
- `perf`: performance improvement
- `build`: build, dependency, packaging, or release plumbing
- `ci`: CI workflow changes
- `chore`: maintenance that does not fit above

Rules:

- Prefer the most specific accurate type over `chore`.
- Use a scope only when it is obvious and helpful.
- Keep the summary imperative, lowercase unless a proper noun requires caps, and under roughly 72 characters before the PR suffix when practical.
- Remove ticket prefixes, branch prefixes, reviewer tags, emoji, and noisy punctuation.
- Include exactly one PR number suffix at the end, such as `(#40)`.
- If the title already contains a PR number elsewhere, remove it and add the canonical suffix at the end.

Examples:

- `feat(orchestration): add task recovery diagnostics (#40)`
- `fix(sync): preserve local skill overrides (#41)`
- `docs: clarify plugin configuration schema (#42)`

## Clean commit body

Write a concise body that explains why the change exists and the meaningful impact. Keep it to 1-3 short paragraphs or bullets.

Remove all of the following:

- `Co-authored-by:` trailers
- `Signed-off-by:` trailers unless the repo explicitly requires DCO signoff
- Generated-by statements, AI attribution lines, or pair-programming credits
- PR template leftovers, empty headings, checklists, screenshots sections, deployment notes with no content
- Long commit lists that repeat the PR commits
- Reviewer discussion, acknowledgements, and co-author descriptions

Keep useful context:

- user-facing behavior changes
- bug cause and fix summary
- compatibility or migration notes
- test or validation summary if important

If there is no useful body after cleanup, use an empty body rather than filler.

## Merge workflow

1. Resolve the PR reference.
2. Fetch and inspect PR metadata.
3. Rebase the PR source branch onto the latest destination branch.
4. Reconcile any rebase conflicts, run relevant validation, and push the rebased source branch with `--force-with-lease` if needed.
5. Refetch PR metadata and confirm the PR is still mergeable.
6. Draft the squash commit title and body.
7. Present the merge plan:
   - PR URL
   - base branch
   - head branch
   - rebase result and whether the source branch was force-pushed with lease
   - review/check status summary
   - final commit title
   - final commit body, or `(empty)`
8. If the user has not already clearly authorized merging, ask for confirmation.
9. Run the squash merge command.
10. Verify the PR is merged.
11. Report the merged PR URL and final commit title.

Command template:

```bash
gh pr merge <number> \
  --repo <owner/repo> \
  --squash \
  --subject "<conventional commit title with PR suffix>" \
  --body "<cleaned commit body>"
```

If the body is empty, pass an empty body intentionally:

```bash
gh pr merge <number> \
  --repo <owner/repo> \
  --squash \
  --subject "<conventional commit title with PR suffix>" \
  --body ""
```

Do not use `--delete-branch` unless the user asks for branch cleanup.

## Verification

After merging, verify with:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --repo <owner/repo> --json state,mergedAt,mergeCommit,url
```

The final response must include:

- whether the PR merged successfully
- the PR URL
- the final squash commit title
- whether the source branch was rebased and whether `--force-with-lease` was used
- whether the body was empty or cleaned
- any warnings, such as pending checks that the user explicitly chose to override

---

# Polaris Logs

Polaris application logs are written to GCP Logs Explorer and exported to BigQuery. This skill provides the **table names, hints for data exploration, and common queries**.

**Always load the `bigquery` skill alongside this one.** It governs how to safely run `bq` queries (SELECT-only, dry runs, cost bounds, etc.). This skill only provides context specific to Polaris logs.

## When to Use

Use this skill whenever someone asks to:

- inspect Polaris logs
- investigate errors
- analyze API request volume or latency
- aggregate logged data
- inspect system activity
- inspect Cloud Run service logs (like "Creative Audit" or "Bid & Budget")

## Environments

Find log database separated by environment:

- "Production" table name: `wpro-bixby2.wpro_bixby2_log_analytics._Default`
- "Test" table name: `prj-npd-plrs-tst-base-mwgr.polaris_log_analytics._AllLogs`

Note that the schemas are similar but not identical, and the available logs differ between environments. Production will eventually match "Test", but for now they differ.

Both environment utilize both `text_payload` and `json_payload` but a similar log message may be in one field or the other depending on the environment, so be sure to check both when exploring.

The Production dataset only includes Polaris API (`api` and `worker`) logs, not Cloud Run service logs. However, Production logs for many Cloud Run services can be manually found outside of BigQuery here: https://console.cloud.google.com/logs/query?project=prj-prd-plrs-backend-cts2

### Containers on "Test" (`resource.type = "k8s_container"`):

| `container_name` | Description          |
| ---------------- | -------------------- |
| `api`            | Polaris API (Django) |
| `nginx`          | nginx access logs    |
| `worker`         | Celery workers       |

Filter example: `JSON_VALUE(resource.labels, "$.container_name") = "worker"`

### Cloud Run services on "Test" (`resource.type = "cloud_run_revision"`):

| `service_name`                              | Description                  |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `runsvc-plrs-tst-bid-budget-optimizer`      | Bid & Budget optimizer       |
| `runsvc-plrs-tst-budget-spend`              | Budget spend processing      |
| `runsvc-plrs-tst-budget-spend-ack`          | Budget spend acknowledgement |
| `runsvc-plrs-tst-creative-audit`            | Creative Audit               |
| `runsvc-plrs-tst-anomaly-detection`         | Anomaly Detection            |
| `runsvc-plrs-tst-reach-planner`             | Reach Planner                |
| `runsvc-plrs-tst-data-imports-email-parser` | Data imports email parser    |
| `runsvc-plrs-tst-webhook-receiver-sendgrid` | SendGrid webhook receiver    |
| `runsvc-platform-webhooks`                  | Platform webhooks            |

Filter example: `JSON_VALUE(resource.labels, "$.service_name") LIKE "%bid-budget%"`

## Example Queries

Swap `TABLE_NAME_HERE` for the target environment.

### Recent rows

```sql
SELECT timestamp, severity, resource.type, json_payload
FROM `TABLE_NAME_HERE`
WHERE
  timestamp > TIMESTAMP_ADD(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL -1 HOUR)
  AND json_payload IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 20
```

### Discover log kinds

```sql
SELECT JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message.kind") AS kind, COUNT(1) AS cnt
FROM `TABLE_NAME_HERE`
WHERE timestamp > TIMESTAMP_ADD(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL -7 DAY)
GROUP BY kind
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 50
```

### Recent Polaris API requests

```sql
SELECT timestamp, severity, json_payload
FROM `TABLE_NAME_HERE`
WHERE
  timestamp > TIMESTAMP_ADD(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL -1 HOUR)
  AND JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message.uri") LIKE "/core/api/%"
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 50
```

### Recent Bid & Budget logs ("Test" only)

```sql
SELECT timestamp, severity, json_payload
FROM `prj-npd-plrs-tst-base-mwgr.polaris_log_analytics._AllLogs` -- Not available in Production's BigQuery
WHERE
  timestamp > TIMESTAMP_ADD(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL -1 DAY)
  AND JSON_VALUE(resource.labels, "$.service_name") LIKE "%bid-budget%"
  AND json_payload IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 50
```

### Count of non-'GET' requests per user

```sql
SELECT
  CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message.user_id") AS INT64) AS user_id,
  COUNT(*) AS request_count
FROM `TABLE_NAME_HERE`
WHERE
  timestamp > TIMESTAMP_ADD(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL -1 DAY)
  AND JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message.event") = "HTTP_RESPONSE"
  AND JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message.method") != "GET"
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY request_count DESC
LIMIT 20
```

### Count of "Task received" per task this morning

```sql
SELECT
  REGEXP_EXTRACT(
    -- support difference of Test and Production
    COALESCE(JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message"), text_payload),
    r"Task ([\w.]+)\[") AS task_name,
  COUNT(*) AS received_count
FROM `TABLE_NAME_HERE`
WHERE
  COALESCE(JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message"), text_payload) LIKE "%Task %received%"
  AND TIME(DATETIME(timestamp, "America/New_York")) BETWEEN TIME "06:00:00" AND TIME "08:00:00"
  AND DATE(DATETIME(timestamp, "America/New_York")) = CURRENT_DATE("America/New_York")
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
```

### Highest latency impact endpoints

Ranked by total time spent (request count × avg latency).

```sql
SELECT
  REGEXP_REPLACE(REGEXP_REPLACE(JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message.uri"), r"/\d+/", "/{ID}/"), r"/C\d+/", "/{CID}/") AS request_url,
  JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message.method") AS request_method,
  COUNT(*) AS request_count,
  ROUND(AVG(CAST(JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message.latency_ms") AS FLOAT64)), 2) AS avg_latency_ms
FROM `TABLE_NAME_HERE`
WHERE
  timestamp > TIMESTAMP_ADD(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL -1 DAY)
  AND JSON_VALUE(json_payload, "$.message.event") = "HTTP_RESPONSE"
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY request_count * avg_latency_ms DESC
LIMIT 25
```

name: postgres
description: PostgreSQL engineering guidance for schema design, query tuning, indexing, migrations, operations, and production troubleshooting. Use when analyzing EXPLAIN plans, optimizing slow queries, designing B-tree/GIN/GiST/BRIN indexes, using JSONB, configuring extensions such as pg_stat_statements, pg_trgm, PostGIS, pgvector, or pgcrypto, tuning VACUUM/autovacuum and statistics, monitoring pg_stat views, investigating locks or bloat, setting up replication, failover, backups, PITR, or reviewing PostgreSQL data-access patterns in application code.
---

# PostgreSQL

Solve PostgreSQL problems from evidence. Prefer small, measurable changes over clever database theater. Production databases are not a vibes-based ecosystem.

## Default workflow

1. Identify the workload, PostgreSQL version, table sizes, cardinality, write/read ratio, latency target, and operational constraints before prescribing changes.
2. Gather evidence with the narrowest safe commands: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, `pg_stat_statements`, `pg_stat_activity`, `pg_stat_user_tables`, `pg_stat_user_indexes`, and relevant schema definitions.
3. Form one hypothesis at a time. Change the query, index, statistics, configuration, or operational setting most directly tied to the evidence.
4. Make production-safe changes by default: prefer concurrent indexes, explicit transactions where appropriate, bounded maintenance windows, rollback notes, and lock impact checks.
5. Verify with before/after plans, timings, buffer counts, row estimates, lock behavior, replication lag, or maintenance metrics.
6. Report the risk, expected impact, validation performed, and any follow-up monitoring needed.

## Reference map

- Read `references/performance.md` for EXPLAIN, indexes, statistics, query rewrites, connection pooling, and configuration tuning.
- Read `references/jsonb.md` for JSONB operators, containment queries, path extraction, expression indexes, generated columns, and JSONB migration patterns.
- Read `references/extensions.md` for pg_stat_statements, pg_trgm, PostGIS, pgvector, pgcrypto, foreign data wrappers, pg_repack, and TimescaleDB.
- Read `references/maintenance.md` for VACUUM, autovacuum, ANALYZE, bloat, pg_stat views, locks, wraparound, and maintenance checks.
- Read `references/replication.md` for streaming replication, logical replication, failover, HA, WAL archiving, backups, and PITR.

## House rules

- Use `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` when optimizing a query, unless running it would mutate data or be unsafe on the target environment.
- Compare estimated rows to actual rows. Bad estimates usually mean statistics, correlation, predicates, or join assumptions are lying.
- Design indexes from observed predicates, joins, ordering, and selectivity. Do not add indexes because they look lonely.
- Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` for production changes when possible. Call out the transaction restrictions.
- Run `ANALYZE` after bulk changes and consider per-column statistics targets for skewed or high-cardinality data.
- Prefer `jsonb` for queryable JSON. Extract hot, validated, or frequently updated values into typed columns or generated columns.
- Prefer `uuid` over `text` for UUID values and `timestamptz` over ambiguous timestamp storage for application events.
- Keep application SQL injection-safe with parameters or prepared statements. Never concatenate user-controlled values into SQL.
- Treat `VACUUM FULL`, table rewrites, blocking DDL, broad locks, and failover steps as high-risk operations that need explicit user confirmation.
- Never disable autovacuum globally. Tune it per table when high-churn tables need different thresholds.

## Common investigation pattern

```sql
-- 1. Find costly query shapes when pg_stat_statements is available.
SELECT query, calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time, rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- 2. Inspect the specific plan with real execution metrics.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, customer_id, status, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1 AND status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

-- 3. Add the smallest index that matches the access pattern, if evidence supports it.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_pending_created_at
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC)
  WHERE status = 'pending';

-- 4. Verify planner behavior and runtime after the change.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, customer_id, status, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1 AND status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

## Handoff

Include the evidence used, exact SQL/config changes proposed or applied, lock and migration risk, verification output, and monitoring follow-up. If a change cannot be safely validated locally, say so instead of pretending the database gods whispered approval.

Use when creating or revising a README, documenting a CLI tool, library, or open source project, or when user asks about README structure, badges, or project documentation. --- # Crafting README.md Files for GitHub > **Core insight:** A README is a sales pitch, onboarding guide, and reference manual compressed into one document. Lead with value, prove with examples, document with precision. ## Why This Matters Most READMEs fail because they: - Bury the value proposition under installation steps - Explain what the tool IS instead of what problem it SOLVES - Lack concrete examples (abstract descriptions don't sell) - Miss the "quick escape hatch" for impatient users (curl one-liner) - Don't show how it compares to alternatives Great READMEs convert scanners into users in under 60 seconds. --- ## THE EXACT PROMPT — README Revision ``` Read the current README.md and dramatically revise it following this structure: 1. Hero section: illustration + badges + one-liner description + curl install 2. TL;DR: "The Problem" + "The Solution" + "Why Use X?" feature table 3. Quick example showing the tool in action (5-10 commands) 4. Design philosophy (3-5 principles with explanations) 5. Comparison table vs alternatives 6. Installation (curl one-liner, package managers, from source) 7. Quick start (numbered steps, copy-paste ready) 8. Command reference (every command with examples) 9. Configuration (full config file example with comments) 10. Architecture diagram (ASCII art showing data flow) 11. Troubleshooting (common errors with fixes) 12. Limitations (honest about what it doesn't do) 13. FAQ (anticipate user questions) Make it comprehensive but scannable. Use tables for comparisons. Show, don't tell. Every claim should have a concrete example. Use ultrathink. ``` --- ## Golden Structure ``` 1. HERO SECTION (above the fold) ├─ Illustration/logo (centered) ├─ Badges (CI, license, version) ├─ One-liner description └─ Quick install (curl | bash) 2. TL;DR (sell the value) ├─ The Problem (pain point) ├─ The Solution (what this does) └─ Why Use X? (feature table) 3. QUICK EXAMPLE (prove it works) └─ 5-10 commands showing core workflow 4. REFERENCE SECTIONS ├─ Design Philosophy ├─ Comparison vs Alternatives ├─ Installation (multiple paths) ├─ Quick Start ├─ Commands ├─ Configuration └─ Architecture 5. SUPPORT SECTIONS ├─ Troubleshooting ├─ Limitations ├─ FAQ ├─ Contributing └─ License ``` --- ## Section Templates ### Hero Section ````markdown # tool-name

Real-World Examples Study these READMEs for patterns: | Project | Notable Pattern | | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | | [xf](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/xf) | Comprehensive CLI docs, search deep-dives | | [ripgrep](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep) | Benchmarks, comparison tables | | [bat](https://github.com/sharkdp/bat) | GIF demos, feature highlights | | [exa](https://github.com/ogham/exa) | Screenshot galleries, color themes | | [starship](https://github.com/starship/starship) | Preset configurations, installation matrix | | [jq](https://github.com/jqlang/jq) | Tutorial progression, manual links | --- ## name: reflect
description: Review recent work and repeated OpenCode workflows to recommend reusable skills, commands, agents, config changes, or playbooks. Use when the user asks to reflect on sessions, improve recurring workflows, identify manual patterns, or decide what should become reusable team configuration.
---

# Reflect

Reflect is an evidence-driven workflow for turning repeated friction into the
smallest useful team asset. The output can be a skill, command, agent tweak,
config change, documentation playbook, or a deliberate decision to change
nothing.

Do not manufacture automation because it would be neat. Neat is how we get a
drawer full of cursed knives.

## When to Use

Use this skill when the user asks to:

- reflect on recent work, a project, or a set of OpenCode sessions;
- find workflows they keep repeating manually;
- identify what should become a reusable skill, command, agent, instruction, or
  config default;
- evaluate whether an existing team asset should be changed;
- improve this OpenCode configuration based on actual usage.

Do not use this for ordinary implementation, one-off debugging, generic
architecture review, or speculative agent creation without evidence.

## Core Rules

- Prefer evidence over vibes.
- Inspect existing assets before proposing new ones.
- Recommend the smallest durable form that solves the repeated problem.
- Treat "do nothing" as a valid result when evidence is weak.
- Ask before editing skills, agents, commands, MCPs, prompts, instructions, or
  config files unless the user explicitly asked for those edits.
- Respect privacy boundaries. Do not inspect unrelated personal files,
  credentials, private messages, browser history, or external accounts unless the
  user explicitly asks and the workflow requires it.
- If OpenCode config-time files change, remind the user to restart OpenCode for
  the change to apply.

## Evidence Sources

Use evidence in this order:

1. The current conversation and explicit user requirements.
2. Current repo guidance such as `AGENTS.md`, `.opencode/`, README files,
   project docs, runbooks, and existing codemaps.
3. Existing team and local OpenCode assets: skills, agents, commands,
   instructions, MCP config, plugin config, and presets.
4. Git history, PR notes, issue references, or release notes when they directly
   explain repeated workflow pain.
5. Recent OpenCode session artifacts only when the user asks for session
   archaeology or clearly approves inspecting them.

## Workflow

### 1. Clarify Scope

Identify the reflection target:

- current session;
- a named workflow, such as PR review, release, Jira ticket work, debugging, or
  onboarding;
- a repository or team configuration area;
- recent OpenCode sessions.

If scope is ambiguous, ask one short clarifying question. If the user says to
reflect broadly, start with the current repo and current conversation before
expanding.

### 2. Inventory Existing Assets

Before proposing anything new, check whether the workflow is already covered by:

- bundled skills under `skill/`;
- bundled commands under `command/`;
- agents under `agent/`;
- instructions under `instruction/` and `manifest.json`;
- MCP definitions under `mcp/`;
- project-local `.opencode/` assets;
- relevant README, runbook, codemap, or `AGENTS.md` guidance.

If an existing asset is close, prefer improving it over adding a near-duplicate.

### 3. Find Repeated Patterns

Look for signals such as:

- the same command sequence repeated across tasks;
- the same context-gathering steps repeated before edits;
- repeated test, build, deploy, release, or QA rituals;
- repeated failures caused by missing instructions or unclear ownership;
- repeated specialist routing decisions;
- repeated user corrections that should become stable guidance.

Strong candidates usually have at least two occurrences, stable inputs, a clear
output, and a clear stopping condition.

### 4. Score Candidates

For each candidate, estimate:

- **Frequency:** how often it appears;
- **Cost:** time, context, money, or attention wasted;
- **Risk:** bugs, unsafe changes, bad reviews, or confusing handoffs;
- **Stability:** whether the inputs and desired output are predictable;
- **Coverage:** whether an existing asset already handles it.

Use confidence labels:

- High: repeated, clear, and already backed by evidence;
- Medium: likely useful but needs one more example or a narrower scope;
- Low: one-off, speculative, or too ambiguous to automate.

### 5. Choose the Smallest Useful Form

Use the least powerful asset that solves the problem:

- **Instruction tweak:** a broad team convention or safety rule.
- **Skill:** reusable workflow guidance for a repeated task shape.
- **Command:** stable manual trigger with predictable inputs.
- **Agent:** distinct specialist role with clear routing and boundaries.
- **Config or MCP change:** safe access/model/routing adjustment.
- **Project playbook:** human-readable process that should not be automated yet.
- **No change:** evidence is weak or an existing asset already covers it.

Avoid creating an agent when a skill is enough. Avoid a skill when a short doc
section is enough. Avoid config changes when the benefit is unclear.

### 6. Propose Before Editing

Unless the user explicitly asked for implementation, present the proposal first:

```text
Findings
- <workflow>: evidence, frequency/confidence, current coverage.

Recommended changes
- <asset/config/doc>: smallest useful change and why.

Skipped
- <candidate>: why it is not worth packaging now.

Needs more evidence
- <candidate>: what would make it actionable.
```

When applying changes, keep them narrow, update tests or docs when applicable,
and avoid broad prompt rules that make agents more eager or expensive.

## Session Archaeology Mode

Only use this mode when the user asks to analyze previous sessions.

1. Locate OpenCode session storage for this machine if available. Prefer documented
   config or storage locations over hard-coded paths.
2. Ask before reading broad cross-repo history if the scope was not explicit.
3. Summarize each session with goal, repo, outcome, friction, commands/tools used,
   and confidence.
4. Cache derived summaries only in an appropriate OpenCode or project-owned
   location, never in random personal directories.
5. Aggregate by recurring themes, not by private content.

Report skipped sessions and errors without stopping the whole analysis.

## Output Format

Return a compact report:

```text
Reflection Report

Scope
- <what was reviewed>

Findings
- <pattern>: evidence, frequency, impact, confidence.

Recommended changes
- <asset/config/doc>: purpose, expected benefit, and why this is the smallest useful form.

Skipped
- <candidate>: reason.

Needs more evidence
- <candidate>: what would confirm it.
```

If nothing qualifies, say:

```text
No strong repeated workflow found. I would not add or change reusable assets yet.
```

# Resolve Project Key

Resolve a Jira project key without stalling the caller. Skills receive context
through prompt text, so callers should state any known project key in plain
language when loading or invoking this helper.

## Steps

1. If the caller or user already provided a project key, normalize it to uppercase and use it directly.
2. Otherwise, read the nearest `AGENTS.md` only if it is already in the current workspace/repo context. Extract an explicit Jira project key if one is documented.
   - Look for labels such as `Jira project`, `Project key`, or `Atlassian Defaults`.
   - Known internal mapping: `bixby2` maps to `BIXB`.
   - Do not search the user's home directory or unrelated parent directories.
3. If still unresolved, check the current git branch name for a Jira project key prefix (e.g. `BIXB-123-fix-thing` → `BIXB`).
4. If still unresolved, return `BIXB`.

Only ask the user when they explicitly requested a non-default project but the
key is ambiguous, or when choosing the wrong project would be destructive. For
normal ticket-writing/listing flows, defaulting to `BIXB` is preferred over
blocking for another prompt.

## Output

A single project key string, e.g. `BIXB`.

name: resolve-test-scope
description: "Internal helper — called by other skills. Determine which files or modules to test based on changed files. Returns one or more test paths."
---

# Resolve Test Scope

Determine the minimal set of test paths based on the files that changed.

## Arguments

- `$1` — Explicit test path override. Optional.

## Steps

1. If `$1` is provided, use it directly.
2. Otherwise, inspect changed files:
   ```bash
   git diff --no-ext-diff --name-only HEAD
   git diff --no-ext-diff --name-only
   git ls-files --others --exclude-standard
   ```
3. Check whether the project's test runner has built-in support for scoping tests to changed files. For example:
   - **Vitest:** `vitest list --changed main` lists test files related to changes vs the base branch.
   - If the test runner provides a changed-file mode, prefer it over manual scope extraction.
4. Read the project's `AGENTS.md` to understand the source layout and test conventions (e.g. Django apps under `bixby2/`, feature modules under `src/features/`, workspace apps under `apps/`).
5. For each changed file, extract the relevant test scope:
   - **Django projects:** the app path (e.g. first two path segments like `bixby2/bid_and_budget/`).
   - **JS/TS projects:** the feature or module directory (e.g. `src/features/dashboard/`).
   - **Monorepos:** the workspace member or app directory (e.g. `apps/budget-spend/`).
   - **Other layouts:** use the nearest test directory or module containing the changed file.
6. Deduplicate the list.
7. If no test paths can be determined, ask the user.

## Output

A list of test paths, e.g. `["bixby2/bid_and_budget/"]` or `["src/features/dashboard/"]`.

# Resolve Ticket Key

Resolve a confirmed Jira ticket key. Skills receive context through prompt text,
so callers should state any known ticket key or Jira URL in plain language when
loading or invoking this helper.

## Steps

1. If the caller or user already provided a ticket key or Jira URL:
   - If it looks like a URL, extract the ticket key from the path (e.g. `PROJ-456` from `https://example.atlassian.net/browse/PROJ-456`).
   - Otherwise normalize and use the ticket key directly.
2. If no ticket key is provided, extract a ticket key from the current branch name:
   ```bash
   git branch --show-current
   ```
   Look for a pattern like `PROJ-12345` (uppercase letters followed by a hyphen and digits) in the branch name.
3. If still unresolved, ask the user for the ticket key and wait.

## Output

A single ticket key string, e.g. `PROJ-456`.

# Skill Creator

A skill for creating new skills and iteratively improving them.

At a high level, the process of creating a skill goes like this:

- Decide what you want the skill to do and roughly how it should do it
- Write a draft of the skill
- Create a few test prompts and run claude-with-access-to-the-skill on them
- Help the user evaluate the results both qualitatively and quantitatively
  - While the runs happen in the background, draft some quantitative evals if there aren't any (if there are some, you can either use as is or modify if you feel something needs to change about them). Then explain them to the user (or if they already existed, explain the ones that already exist)
  - Use the `eval-viewer/generate_review.py` script to show the user the results for them to look at, and also let them look at the quantitative metrics
- Rewrite the skill based on feedback from the user's evaluation of the results (and also if there are any glaring flaws that become apparent from the quantitative benchmarks)
- Repeat until you're satisfied
- Expand the test set and try again at larger scale

Your job when using this skill is to figure out where the user is in this process and then jump in and help them progress through these stages. So for instance, maybe they're like "I want to make a skill for X". You can help narrow down what they mean, write a draft, write the test cases, figure out how they want to evaluate, run all the prompts, and repeat.

On the other hand, maybe they already have a draft of the skill. In this case you can go straight to the eval/iterate part of the loop.

Of course, you should always be flexible and if the user is like "I don't need to run a bunch of evaluations, just vibe with me", you can do that instead.

Then after the skill is done (but again, the order is flexible), you can also run the skill description improver, which we have a whole separate script for, to optimize the triggering of the skill.

Cool? Cool.

## Communicating with the user

The skill creator is liable to be used by people across a wide range of familiarity with coding jargon. If you haven't heard (and how could you, it's only very recently that it started), there's a trend now where the power of Claude is inspiring plumbers to open up their terminals, parents and grandparents to google "how to install npm". On the other hand, the bulk of users are probably fairly computer-literate.

So please pay attention to context cues to understand how to phrase your communication! In the default case, just to give you some idea:

- "evaluation" and "benchmark" are borderline, but OK
- for "JSON" and "assertion" you want to see serious cues from the user that they know what those things are before using them without explaining them

It's OK to briefly explain terms if you're in doubt, and feel free to clarify terms with a short definition if you're unsure if the user will get it.

## Creating a skill

### Capture Intent

Start by understanding the user's intent. The current conversation might already contain a workflow the user wants to capture (e.g., they say "turn this into a skill"). If so, extract answers from the conversation history first — the tools used, the sequence of steps, corrections the user made, input/output formats observed. The user may need to fill the gaps, and should confirm before proceeding to the next step.

1. What should this skill enable Claude to do?
2. When should this skill trigger? (what user phrases/contexts)
3. What's the expected output format?
4. Should we set up test cases to verify the skill works? Skills with objectively verifiable outputs (file transforms, data extraction, code generation, fixed workflow steps) benefit from test cases. Skills with subjective outputs (writing style, art) often don't need them. Suggest the appropriate default based on the skill type, but let the user decide.

### Interview and Research

Proactively ask questions about edge cases, input/output formats, example files, success criteria, and dependencies. Wait to write test prompts until you've got this part ironed out.

Check available MCPs - if useful for research (searching docs, finding similar skills, looking up best practices), research in parallel via subagents if available, otherwise inline. Come prepared with context to reduce burden on the user.

### Write the SKILL.md

Based on the user interview, fill in these components:

- **name**: Skill identifier
- **description**: When to trigger, what it does. This is the primary triggering mechanism - include both what the skill does AND specific contexts for when to use it. All "when to use" info goes here, not in the body. Note: currently Claude has a tendency to "undertrigger" skills -- to not use them when they'd be useful. To combat this, please make the skill descriptions a little bit "pushy". So for instance, instead of "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data.", you might write "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions dashboards, data visualization, internal metrics, or wants to display any kind of company data, even if they don't explicitly ask for a 'dashboard.'"
- **compatibility**: Required tools, dependencies (optional, rarely needed)
- **the rest of the skill :)**

### Skill Writing Guide

#### Anatomy of a Skill

```
skill-name/
├── SKILL.md (required)
│   ├── YAML frontmatter (name, description required)
│   └── Markdown instructions
└── Bundled Resources (optional)
    ├── scripts/    - Executable code for deterministic/repetitive tasks
    ├── references/ - Docs loaded into context as needed
    └── assets/     - Files used in output (templates, icons, fonts)
```

#### Progressive Disclosure

Skills use a three-level loading system:
1. **Metadata** (name + description) - Always in context (~100 words)
2. **SKILL.md body** - In context whenever skill triggers (<500 lines ideal)
3. **Bundled resources** - As needed (unlimited, scripts can execute without loading)

These word counts are approximate and you can feel free to go longer if needed.

**Key patterns:**
- Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines; if you're approaching this limit, add an additional layer of hierarchy along with clear pointers about where the model using the skill should go next to follow up.
- Reference files clearly from SKILL.md with guidance on when to read them
- For large reference files (>300 lines), include a table of contents

**Domain organization**: When a skill supports multiple domains/frameworks, organize by variant:
```
cloud-deploy/
├── SKILL.md (workflow + selection)
└── references/
    ├── aws.md
    ├── gcp.md
    └── azure.md
```
Claude reads only the relevant reference file.

#### Principle of Lack of Surprise

This goes without saying, but skills must not contain malware, exploit code, or any content that could compromise system security. A skill's contents should not surprise the user in their intent if described. Don't go along with requests to create misleading skills or skills designed to facilitate unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or other malicious activities. Things like a "roleplay as an XYZ" are OK though.

#### Writing Patterns

Prefer using the imperative form in instructions.

**Defining output formats** - You can do it like this:
```markdown
## Report structure
ALWAYS use this exact template:
# [Title]
## Executive summary
## Key findings
## Recommendations
```

**Examples pattern** - It's useful to include examples. You can format them like this (but if "Input" and "Output" are in the examples you might want to deviate a little):
```markdown
## Commit message format
**Example 1:**
Input: Added user authentication with JWT tokens
Output: feat(auth): implement JWT-based authentication
```

### Writing Style

Try to explain to the model why things are important in lieu of heavy-handed musty MUSTs. Use theory of mind and try to make the skill general and not super-narrow to specific examples. Start by writing a draft and then look at it with fresh eyes and improve it.

### Test Cases

After writing the skill draft, come up with 2-3 realistic test prompts — the kind of thing a real user would actually say. Share them with the user: [you don't have to use this exact language] "Here are a few test cases I'd like to try. Do these look right, or do you want to add more?" Then run them.

Save test cases to `evals/evals.json`. Don't write assertions yet — just the prompts. You'll draft assertions in the next step while the runs are in progress.

```json
{
  "skill_name": "example-skill",
  "evals": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "prompt": "User's task prompt",
      "expected_output": "Description of expected result",
      "files": []
    }
  ]
}
```

See `references/schemas.md` for the full schema (including the `assertions` field, which you'll add later).

## Running and evaluating test cases

This section is one continuous sequence — don't stop partway through. Do NOT use `/skill-test` or any other testing skill.

Put results in `<skill-name>-workspace/` as a sibling to the skill directory. Within the workspace, organize results by iteration (`iteration-1/`, `iteration-2/`, etc.) and within that, each test case gets a directory (`eval-0/`, `eval-1/`, etc.). Don't create all of this upfront — just create directories as you go.

### Step 1: Spawn all runs (with-skill AND baseline) in the same turn

For each test case, spawn two subagents in the same turn — one with the skill, one without. This is important: don't spawn the with-skill runs first and then come back for baselines later. Launch everything at once so it all finishes around the same time.

**With-skill run:**

```
Execute this task:
- Skill path: <path-to-skill>
- Task: <eval prompt>
- Input files: <eval files if any, or "none">
- Save outputs to: <workspace>/iteration-<N>/eval-<ID>/with_skill/outputs/
- Outputs to save: <what the user cares about — e.g., "the .docx file", "the final CSV">
```

**Baseline run** (same prompt, but the baseline depends on context):
- **Creating a new skill**: no skill at all. Same prompt, no skill path, save to `without_skill/outputs/`.
- **Improving an existing skill**: the old version. Before editing, snapshot the skill (`cp -r <skill-path> <workspace>/skill-snapshot/`), then point the baseline subagent at the snapshot. Save to `old_skill/outputs/`.

Write an `eval_metadata.json` for each test case (assertions can be empty for now). Give each eval a descriptive name based on what it's testing — not just "eval-0". Use this name for the directory too. If this iteration uses new or modified eval prompts, create these files for each new eval directory — don't assume they carry over from previous iterations.

```json
{
  "eval_id": 0,
  "eval_name": "descriptive-name-here",
  "prompt": "The user's task prompt",
  "assertions": []
}
```

### Step 2: While runs are in progress, draft assertions

Don't just wait for the runs to finish — you can use this time productively. Draft quantitative assertions for each test case and explain them to the user. If assertions already exist in `evals/evals.json`, review them and explain what they check.

Good assertions are objectively verifiable and have descriptive names — they should read clearly in the benchmark viewer so someone glancing at the results immediately understands what each one checks. Subjective skills (writing style, design quality) are better evaluated qualitatively — don't force assertions onto things that need human judgment.

Update the `eval_metadata.json` files and `evals/evals.json` with the assertions once drafted. Also explain to the user what they'll see in the viewer — both the qualitative outputs and the quantitative benchmark.

### Step 3: As runs complete, capture timing data

When each subagent task completes, you receive a notification containing `total_tokens` and `duration_ms`. Save this data immediately to `timing.json` in the run directory:

```json
{
  "total_tokens": 84852,
  "duration_ms": 23332,
  "total_duration_seconds": 23.3
}
```

This is the only opportunity to capture this data — it comes through the task notification and isn't persisted elsewhere. Process each notification as it arrives rather than trying to batch them.

### Step 4: Grade, aggregate, and launch the viewer

Once all runs are done:

1. **Grade each run** — spawn a grader subagent (or grade inline) that reads `agents/grader.md` and evaluates each assertion against the outputs. Save results to `grading.json` in each run directory. The grading.json expectations array must use the fields `text`, `passed`, and `evidence` (not `name`/`met`/`details` or other variants) — the viewer depends on these exact field names. For assertions that can be checked programmatically, write and run a script rather than eyeballing it — scripts are faster, more reliable, and can be reused across iterations.

2. **Aggregate into benchmark** — run the aggregation script from the skill-creator directory:
   ```bash
   python -m scripts.aggregate_benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N --skill-name <name>
   ```
   This produces `benchmark.json` and `benchmark.md` with pass_rate, time, and tokens for each configuration, with mean ± stddev and the delta. If generating benchmark.json manually, see `references/schemas.md` for the exact schema the viewer expects.
Put each with_skill version before its baseline counterpart.

3. **Do an analyst pass** — read the benchmark data and surface patterns the aggregate stats might hide. See `agents/analyzer.md` (the "Analyzing Benchmark Results" section) for what to look for — things like assertions that always pass regardless of skill (non-discriminating), high-variance evals (possibly flaky), and time/token tradeoffs.

4. **Launch the viewer** with both qualitative outputs and quantitative data:
   ```bash
   nohup python <skill-creator-path>/eval-viewer/generate_review.py \
     <workspace>/iteration-N \
     --skill-name "my-skill" \
     --benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N/benchmark.json \
     > /dev/null 2>&1 &
   VIEWER_PID=$!
   ```
   For iteration 2+, also pass `--previous-workspace <workspace>/iteration-<N-1>`.

   **Cowork / headless environments:** If `webbrowser.open()` is not available or the environment has no display, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Feedback will be downloaded as a `feedback.json` file when the user clicks "Submit All Reviews". After download, copy `feedback.json` into the workspace directory for the next iteration to pick up.

Note: please use generate_review.py to create the viewer; there's no need to write custom HTML.

5. **Tell the user** something like: "I've opened the results in your browser. There are two tabs — 'Outputs' lets you click through each test case and leave feedback, 'Benchmark' shows the quantitative comparison. When you're done, come back here and let me know."

### What the user sees in the viewer

The "Outputs" tab shows one test case at a time:
- **Prompt**: the task that was given
- **Output**: the files the skill produced, rendered inline where possible
- **Previous Output** (iteration 2+): collapsed section showing last iteration's output
- **Formal Grades** (if grading was run): collapsed section showing assertion pass/fail
- **Feedback**: a textbox that auto-saves as they type
- **Previous Feedback** (iteration 2+): their comments from last time, shown below the textbox

The "Benchmark" tab shows the stats summary: pass rates, timing, and token usage for each configuration, with per-eval breakdowns and analyst observations.

Navigation is via prev/next buttons or arrow keys. When done, they click "Submit All Reviews" which saves all feedback to `feedback.json`.

## Improving the skill

This is the heart of the loop. You've run the test cases, the user has reviewed the results, and now you need to make the skill better based on their feedback.

### How to think about improvements

1. **Generalize from the feedback.** The big picture thing that's happening here is that we're trying to create skills that can be used a million times (maybe literally, maybe even more who knows) across many different prompts. Here you and the user are iterating on only a few examples over and over again because it helps move faster. The user knows these examples in and out and it's quick for them to assess new outputs. But if the skill you and the user are codeveloping works only for those examples, it's useless. Rather than put in fiddly overfitty changes, or oppressively constrictive MUSTs, if there's some stubborn issue, you might try branching out and using different metaphors, or recommending different patterns of working. It's relatively cheap to try and maybe you'll land on something great.

2. **Keep the prompt lean.** Remove things that aren't pulling their weight. Make sure to read the transcripts, not just the final outputs — if it looks like the skill is making the model waste a bunch of time doing things that are unproductive, you can try getting rid of the parts of the skill that are making it do that and seeing what happens.

3. **Explain the why.** Try hard to explain the **why** behind everything you're asking the model to do. Today's LLMs are *smart*. They have good theory of mind and when given a good harness can go beyond rote instructions and really make things happen. Even if the feedback from the user is terse or frustrated, try to actually understand the task and why the user is writing what they wrote, and what they actually wrote, and then transmit this understanding into the instructions. If you find yourself writing ALWAYS or NEVER in all caps, or using super rigid structures, that's a yellow flag — if possible, reframe and explain the reasoning so that the model understands why the thing you're asking for is important. That's a more humane, powerful, and effective approach.

4. **Look for repeated work across test cases.** Read the transcripts from the test runs and notice if the subagents all independently wrote similar helper scripts or took the same multi-step approach to something. If all 3 test cases resulted in the subagent writing a `create_docx.py` or a `build_chart.py`, that's a strong signal the skill should bundle that script. Write it once, put it in `scripts/`, and tell the skill to use it. This saves every future invocation from reinventing the wheel.

This task is pretty important (we are trying to create billions a year in economic value here!) and your thinking time is not the blocker; take your time and really mull things over. I'd suggest writing a draft revision and then looking at it anew and making improvements. Really do your best to get into the head of the user and understand what they want and need.

### The iteration loop

After improving the skill:

1. Apply your improvements to the skill
2. Rerun all test cases into a new `iteration-<N+1>/` directory, including baseline runs. If you're creating a new skill, the baseline is always `without_skill` (no skill) — that stays the same across iterations. If you're improving an existing skill, use your judgment on what makes sense as the baseline: the original version the user came in with, or the previous iteration.
3. Launch the reviewer with `--previous-workspace` pointing at the previous iteration
4. Wait for the user to review and tell you they're done
5. Read the new feedback, improve again, repeat

This handles the full optimization loop automatically. It splits the eval set into 60% train and 40% held-out test, evaluates the current description (running each query 3 times to get a reliable trigger rate), then calls Claude to propose improvements based on what failed. It re-evaluates each new description on both train and test, iterating up to 5 times. When it's done, it opens an HTML report in the browser showing the results per iteration and returns JSON with `best_description` — selected by test score rather than train score to avoid overfitting.

### How skill triggering works

Understanding the triggering mechanism helps design better eval queries. Skills appear in Claude's `available_skills` list with their name + description, and Claude decides whether to consult a skill based on that description. The important thing to know is that Claude only consults skills for tasks it can't easily handle on its own — simple, one-step queries like "read this PDF" may not trigger a skill even if the description matches perfectly, because Claude can handle them directly with basic tools. Complex, multi-step, or specialized queries reliably trigger skills when the description matches.

This means your eval queries should be substantive enough that Claude would actually benefit from consulting a skill. Simple queries like "read file X" are poor test cases — they won't trigger skills regardless of description quality.

### Step 4: Apply the result

Take `best_description` from the JSON output and update the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter. Show the user before/after and report the scores.

## Claude.ai-specific instructions

In Claude.ai, the core workflow is the same (draft → test → review → improve → repeat), but because Claude.ai doesn't have subagents, some mechanics change. Here's what to adapt:

**Running test cases**: No subagents means no parallel execution. For each test case, read the skill's SKILL.md, then follow its instructions to accomplish the test prompt yourself. Do them one at a time. This is less rigorous than independent subagents (you wrote the skill and you're also running it, so you have full context), but it's a useful sanity check — and the human review step compensates. Skip the baseline runs — just use the skill to complete the task as requested.

**Reviewing results**: If you can't open a browser (e.g., Claude.ai's VM has no display, or you're on a remote server), skip the browser reviewer entirely. Instead, present results directly in the conversation. For each test case, show the prompt and the output. If the output is a file the user needs to see (like a .docx or .xlsx), save it to the filesystem and tell them where it is so they can download and inspect it. Ask for feedback inline: "How does this look? Anything you'd change?"

**Benchmarking**: Skip the quantitative benchmarking — it relies on baseline comparisons which aren't meaningful without subagents. Focus on qualitative feedback from the user.

**The iteration loop**: Same as before — improve the skill, rerun the test cases, ask for feedback — just without the browser reviewer in the middle. You can still organize results into iteration directories on the filesystem if you have one.

**Description optimization**: This section requires the `claude` CLI tool (specifically `claude -p`) which is only available in Claude Code. Skip it if you're on Claude.ai.

**Blind comparison**: Requires subagents. Skip it.

**Packaging**: The `package_skill.py` script works anywhere with Python and a filesystem. On Claude.ai, you can run it and the user can download the resulting `.skill` file.

**Updating an existing skill**: The user might be asking you to update an existing skill, not create a new one. In this case:
- **Preserve the original name.** Note the skill's directory name and `name` frontmatter field -- use them unchanged. E.g., if the installed skill is `research-helper`, output `research-helper.skill` (not `research-helper-v2`).
- **Copy to a writeable location before editing.** The installed skill path may be read-only. Copy to `/tmp/skill-name/`, edit there, and package from the copy.
- **If packaging manually, stage in `/tmp/` first**, then copy to the output directory -- direct writes may fail due to permissions.

## Cowork-Specific Instructions

If you're in Cowork, the main things to know are:

- You have subagents, so the main workflow (spawn test cases in parallel, run baselines, grade, etc.) all works. (However, if you run into severe problems with timeouts, it's OK to run the test prompts in series rather than parallel.)
- You don't have a browser or display, so when generating the eval viewer, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Then proffer a link that the user can click to open the HTML in their browser.
- For whatever reason, the Cowork setup seems to disincline Claude from generating the eval viewer after running the tests, so just to reiterate: whether you're in Cowork or in Claude Code, after running tests, you should always generate the eval viewer for the human to look at examples before revising the skill yourself and trying to make corrections, using `generate_review.py` (not writing your own boutique html code).
